posts.title: Kotlin Heroes: Episode 15 – Anniversary Edition
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Kotlin turned 15 this year, and we’re celebrating with the 15th episode of Kotlin Heroes! 💜
Kotlin Heroes is a series of online programming contests, where participants solve algorithmic problems using Kotlin. Whether you’re new to the language or an experienced programmer, it’s a chance to practice your Kotlin skills, challenge yourself, and have some fun along the way.
Over the past 14 episodes, Kotlin Heroes has attracted nearly 190,000 registrations across practice rounds and contests. A big thank-you to everyone who’s been part of this journey!
The next contest takes place on December 8, 2026, and the practice round will open on December 1, 2026. Join us for this anniversary edition and get a chance to win an exclusive Kotlin Heroes anniversary T-shirt!
Join Kotlin Heroes: Episode 15
How it works
Warm up in the practice round. Get familiar with the contest format, solve training problems, and use available hints and solutions whenever you need help.
Compete on December 8. You’ll have 2 hours and 30 minutes to tackle problems ranging from beginner-friendly tasks to challenges for experienced competitive programmers.
Win prizes! Top participants will receive cash prizes and exclusive anniversary T-shirts. Plus, everyone who solves at least one problem in the main contest has a chance to win a T-shirt in the raffle.
Why join?
Learning a new programming language is a valuable skill, and one of the best ways to improve is to solve problems yourself.
With AI becoming part of everyday programming, Kotlin Heroes is an opportunity to celebrate human problem-solving, challenge yourself, and discover what you can accomplish with Kotlin!
Prizes
You don’t have to finish at the top of the leaderboard to win something!
🥇 1st place: $512
🥈 2nd place: $256
🥉 3rd place: $128
🎽 Top 50 participants: Exclusive Kotlin Heroes 15th anniversary T-shirts
🎁 50 additional anniversary T-shirts: Raffled among participants who solve at least one problem
Get ready for the contest
Watch our Kotlin in Competitive Programming playlist for tips from experienced competitive programmers.
Read the Kotlin competitive programming tutorial.
Explore previous Kotlin Heroes contest solutions, including Episode 12, Episode 13, and Episode 14.
A note on fair play: Kotlin Heroes is about testing your own problem-solving skills. AI-assisted problem solving is restricted during the main contest, so please review the Codeforces AI usage rules before participating. Let’s keep the competition fair and enjoyable for everyone!
Register for Kotlin Heroes: Episode 15
See you on December 8, and good luck!

posts.title: GoLand Intelligence Now Available in Cursor and VS Code
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
What if you could use GoLand’s language intelligence outside the IDE, across multiple development environments? Today, we’re taking the first step toward making this possible by releasing a public preview of the Go by GoLand LSP – an extension for VS Code-based editors, including Cursor. This will bring GoLand intelligence beyond the IntelliJ Platform, making it available to all developers, whatever their workflows look like. In this announcement, we’d like to share what the Go by GoLand LSP is, why we’re releasing it now, and what we have planned for the future.
Go by GoLand is an extension for VS Code-based editors based on language server and debug adapter protocols (LSP and DAP). These open protocols allow code editors and agents to use language-specific features for editing and debugging independently of any particular development environment. This way, developers can benefit from the language intelligence and tools they know from dedicated IDEs, such as GoLand, in general-purpose editors, such as VS Code.
This public preview is a free Beta version that provides some of GoLand’s capabilities (more on that in What you can do in this preview). We’re releasing it to the public to gather your feedback on its performance and hear your feature requests, so that we can continue our work on this project in a way that meets your real needs.
Code happens in more than one place
As new tools and workflows emerge, development keeps happening in more than one place. In 2026, almost all Gophers (98.2%) use coding agents1, and 82% of them work with agents across two or more surfaces: the IDE, a terminal, or remote cloud environments1.
While we recognize this shift toward agentic development, we believe one thing hasn’t changed and will not change: It’s still the developers who own the resulting code and take responsibility for it. Only 8% of Go developers rarely or never review AI-generated code1. For those who do, strong language support is still essential, and that’s where a deep understanding of Go matters the most.
For years, GoLand has been appreciated for its superior project-wide search, indexing, refactoring, and debugging capabilities, especially in large codebases and monorepos. As these features become increasingly more important for navigating and understanding the code you own, we believe all developers should have access to them – wherever they Go.
That’s why we want to bring GoLand intelligence beyond the IntelliJ Platform. Making it available in VS Code-based editors is the first step on that journey.
Understanding the whole project
JetBrains, and the Go Ecosystem team in particular, have extensive experience working with customers who have very large codebases or monorepos spanning millions of lines of code. This is the scenario where we know GoLand offers the most value. When developing the Go by GoLand LSP, we focused on what we know best: providing a reliable and reasonably fast experience in projects of all sizes without overconsuming resources.
Our LSP analyzes the project as a whole, not in isolated pieces, so it can provide complete information about the project and its context.
We benchmarked the LSP on a repository with almost 93 million lines of code across 34 modules, more than double the size of the Linux kernel. In our tests, jumping to a definition was virtually instant at 11 ms, which is faster than a single frame on a 60 Hz display. Finding every implementation across all 34 modules took 13 seconds, and the server used 833 MiB of memory throughout, roughly 5% of a 16 GB laptop’s RAM.
We’re continuing to measure and improve our LSP benchmarks.
What you can do in this preview
As this is the first public preview of the Go by GoLand LSP, its capabilities are currently limited. We’ll be adding more features in later builds. We rely on your feedback to learn which features you would find most helpful, so we can prioritize them.
At the moment, the LSP supports:
Code navigation: Jump to definitions and implementations, find all usages, and explore call and type hierarchies across your entire project.
Code analysis: Catch problems with inspections, including data flow analysis, and apply quick-fixes.
Refactoring: Rename and move symbols safely across the codebase.
Running: Build and run Go packages, save launch configurations for repeat runs.
Debugging: Set breakpoints, step through code, and inspect variables.
Testing: Run and debug tests directly from the editor.
Signature help: get suggestions as you type, see call parameters while you fill in its arguments.
Documentation on hover: Hover over a symbol to read its documentation without leaving your code.
Code completion: Get suggestions for references, import paths, package names, keywords, method receivers, and more.
You can find the full, up-to-date list of features in the documentation.
How to get started
If you’d like to try any of these features, here’s how to start using the Go by GoLand LSP in Visual Studio Code or Cursor:
Install Go and make sure that the go executable is in your system PATH.
Disable the Go extension by the Go team if you have it, because two language servers on one file give you duplicate results.
Open the Extensions view in Visual Studio Code or in Cursor, search for Go by GoLand, and click Install.
Open any Go file in your project, and the extension immediately imports your modules and analyzes the project.
When you open a Go source file for the first time, the End User License Agreement (EULA) opens in a separate editor tab. Accept the agreement to use the extension. If you close the tab without accepting the agreement, it opens again the next time you open a project.
Licensing
During the preview period, you can use the extension for free without a license. Each preview build expires 30 days after its release. To renew the evaluation period, you have to install a newer preview version.
What’s next
Not only people can benefit from the code intelligence you could previously find only in GoLand. It can make coding agents more efficient, too, by cutting costs, speeding up development, and improving code quality. That’s why we’re working to make it easier for agents to use this extension as well.
We’ve already seen this approach bring material improvements at Netflix, where benchmarks showed that an integration with a JetBrains’ code engine helped agents complete real programming tasks using fewer tokens and less time. Stay tuned for more updates!
Help us decide what comes next
The public preview is now available for free in VS Code and Cursor. We encourage you to try it on your project and look forward to hearing your feedback about what works well, what doesn’t, and what we should include next. You can share your thoughts on the GoLand Slack channel or using this form.
Please remember that while we’ve made every effort to ensure the extension is suitable for regular development work, it is still a pre-release that may contain bugs. Reporting issues you experience in your workflows will help us deliver a stable 1.0 release.
Thank you for helping us bring GoLand intelligence wherever you Go.
Happy coding,
Sergey Larionov
Head of Go Ecosystem at JetBrains

1 JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem Report 2026

posts.title: Qodana 2026.3 Release: What’s New
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Qodana 2026.3 release brings Dart and Flutter projects into Qodana, so you can review code analysis findings together with your team. Baseline matching is now more accurate: In targeted validation across four scenarios, average precision rose from 45% to 90%. Qodana is better at recognizing an existing issue after a file move, rename, or refactoring, helping quality gates stay focused on new problems.
There’s more to explore on the security side. New .NET checks help you find cryptographic algorithms and SSL protocols that need a closer look as you plan for post-quantum security. Qodana can now follow untrusted input through Spring applications, while improved inspections for JavaScript, TypeScript, and C# produce fewer false alarms.
Try Qodana
Table of Contents

Dart and Flutter code analysis
A new baseline algorithm for more accurate issue matching
Deeper security analysis
Post-quantum cryptography inspections for .NET
Spring-aware taint analysis
OpenGrep taint analysis without a trace limit
More precise security inspections for JavaScript, TypeScript, and C#
What to do next


Dart and Flutter code analysis
Building a Dart or Flutter app? You can now analyze it with Qodana. When the Dart analyzer flags a problem, the Qodana report shows the affected code and explains what happened. Your team can review those findings together, decide what to address, and see what changes over time.
In the first illustrative example, Qodana reports a dead_code_on_catch_subtype diagnostic in backup_restorer.dart. A general IOException handler comes before a FileSystemException handler, so the more specific handler can never run. The report highlights the unreachable block and explains why it will be skipped.




The second example shows an unreachable_switch_case diagnostic in job_queue.dart. Earlier patterns already cover the restore case, so that branch will never execute. Qodana points to the affected case and shows the analyzer’s explanation in the report.




Run Qodana 2026.3 on a Dart or Flutter project to see these diagnostics alongside your code and review the findings with your team.
A new baseline algorithm for more accurate issue matching
A file move, rename, or refactoring can make an old finding look like a new one. Qodana 2026.3 is better at recognizing when a given finding has come up before, so your quality gate can focus solely on issues that arose during the latest development cycle. An extended hash cascade and an improved matching algorithm make this possible. The improvement is currently available for Java, Kotlin, JavaScript, and TypeScript, with more languages to follow.
We tested this on findings that are easy to misclassify after code changes. The tables show how often Qodana recognizes an existing finding or identifies a new one. They measure baseline matching, not whether an inspection catches a defect. All differences are shown in percentage points.
Java and Kotlin: 889 findings from five months of incremental analysis of the Ultimate monorepo (January – May 2026), limited to changed files.

StateMetricOldNewΔ (pp)
UnchangedPrecision52.49%95.30%+42.81
UnchangedRecall28.96%91.61%+62.65
UnchangedF137.33%93.42%+56.09
NewPrecision77.18%96.55%+19.37
NewRecall96.72%97.67%+0.95
NewF185.85%97.10%+11.25





JavaScript and TypeScript: 359 findings from four months of analysis of the open-source Next.js repository (May – August 2026).

StateMetricOldNewΔ (pp)
UnchangedPrecision16.67%86.65%+69.98
UnchangedRecall2.25%80.63%+78.38
UnchangedF13.97%83.06%+79.09
NewPrecision33.40%82.61%+49.21
NewRecall94.19%88.37%−5.82
NewF148.41%85.39%+36.98





The biggest improvement is in recognizing findings that have come up in previous analyses, even when the surrounding code has changed. Matching of new findings improved overall, too. The tables also show a trade-off: for JavaScript and TypeScript, recall for new findings is lower, even though precision and F1 have improved.
The code examples show why matching is difficult. The original finding is attached to a condition that is always true. The following changes move or rename the file and refactor the surrounding code, while the underlying problem remains.
Original code, where the condition is always true:




After a file move and a small refactoring:




After a file rename:




After a larger refactoring that moves the condition into another method:




On your first Qodana 2026.3 run with an existing baseline, review how findings are classified after file moves or refactorings and check the quality gate result. This is especially useful for teams whose CI pipelines depend on the distinction between new and existing problems.
Deeper security analysis
In the last release, we introduced post-quantum checks for JVM projects and made the SABER benchmarks public. Now those checks are also available for .NET projects, Spring analysis can follow untrusted input through Java applications, and existing security inspections produce fewer false alarms.
Post-quantum cryptography inspections for .NET
Before you can plan a move to post-quantum security, you need to know which algorithms and protocols your .NET code uses. Qodana 2026.3 helps you find them. Its new inspections flag algorithms that are not post-quantum compatible and detect pre-quantum SSL protocols. They also show the algorithms used in your code and their NIST security ratings.
The example below shows a finding next to the affected .NET code, with an explanation you can use to review it.




To try it, analyze a .NET project with Qodana 2026.3 and review the security findings for algorithm and SSL protocol usage.
Spring-aware taint analysis
A value can enter a Spring application through an HTTP request and travel through the code before reaching a SQL query. Qodana 2026.3 can now follow that path. It recognizes annotations such as @RequestParam as sources of untrusted input and reports paths that could lead to a security issue. The example below shows one such path flagged as a potential SQL injection.




What can a PDF conversion endpoint reveal about AI-generated code? In our companion case study, Qodana follows a JSON request value from Spring’s @RequestBody through DocumentController and DocumentService to a ProcessBuilder shell command. Read the full case study to see the trace, why the path matters, and how the conversion could be made safer.
OpenGrep taint analysis without a trace limit
To identify risky data flows, taint analysis follows a trace: one possible route from untrusted input to a sensitive operation. Branches and function calls can create many such routes through an application. Previously, Qodana’s OpenGrep-powered inspection had a default limit of 100 traces. The limit helped keep analysis time under control, but once it was reached, any additional paths went unchecked.
In Qodana 2026.3, we reduced the time needed to process each trace and removed the limit. Qodana can now examine more paths while keeping overall analysis time roughly comparable. For developers and security teams, this means broader coverage of complex data flows and fewer paths left unchecked because of a fixed threshold.
More precise security inspections for JavaScript, TypeScript, and C#
We ran the same SABER benchmark projects against both releases to see how the updated JavaScript, TypeScript, and C# inspections performed. The comparison below shows more known benchmark issues found and fewer false alarms.




This leaves security teams with fewer alerts to sort through. Results vary by benchmark, and SABER does not report TypeScript separately.
Explore the full benchmark for project-level results and individual reports.
What to do next
Already using Qodana? These features are available now. On your next run, see how the baseline handles findings after a move or refactoring, and explore the new checks that apply to your project.
New to Qodana? See the analysis workflow in a demo and find out which of these checks would be useful for your team.
Book a demo
Get more practical insights on code quality and security. Subscribe to the Qodana blog for new posts.

posts.title: YouTrack Adds More Ways to Use AI on Your Terms
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
YouTrack 2026.3 introduces Ask YouTrack, a new built-in agentic AI chat, where you can ask questions in natural language and take action on tasks, tickets, and articles. You can connect your preferred AI models, and administrators can monitor token usage by user. While this release expands what you can do with AI in YouTrack, using it remains optional. Organizations that prefer to work without AI can disable it entirely. 
For teams that work with Slack, the YouTrack Slack app can now use AI to create tasks from threads. We’ve also simplified MCP setup, so teams can connect YouTrack Cloud to Claude and ChatGPT directly through their respective directories, without manual configuration.
Beyond AI, discover improved planning with Whiteboards and Gantt charts, an enhanced reporter experience in YouTrack Helpdesk, and new YouTrack apps from JetBrains Marketplace.
AI on your terms
As we shared in our AI vision blog post, we believe whether and how to use AI should be your decision, not ours. YouTrack doesn’t push AI into every workflow. You can choose the capabilities that meet your needs or turn AI off entirely.
This release expands your options. Two ways to work with AI in YouTrack are already available: MCP connections that let you work with YouTrack from external AI tools, IDEs, and agents, and the built-in AI Assistant that helps you summarize content and write faster. Now there’s a third: Ask YouTrack, an agentic AI chat built into YouTrack, with a choice of providers and models to fit your organization’s policies and budget.




Ask YouTrack: Your built-in agentic AI chat
Ask YouTrack can assist you right where you work in YouTrack. It supports models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, as well as local models compatible with these providers. 
Because Ask YouTrack is built into the product and works directly with your YouTrack context, it uses tokens more efficiently than a setup that runs entirely through MCP. It currently supports actions involving tasks, tickets, and articles, with more capabilities coming soon.
Manage tasks, tickets, and knowledge in one chat
Find and organize tasks across projects
Search across projects, get answers, and gain insights into ongoing work using natural-language prompts. For example, software teams can use Ask YouTrack to find unresolved bugs related to an upcoming release and group them by feature or subsystem. The results can then be visualized and summarized in an article for everyone involved in the release.




Turn answers into work actions
While reviewing a task, for example, managers can ask what’s holding the task up and get an answer based on the available YouTrack context. They can then switch to the full-screen chat to organize workloads, review deadlines, and reassign tasks in bulk. Chats are saved, so you can return to them later.




Manage tickets and reply to customers
Support agents working with helpdesk projects can use Ask YouTrack to find tickets by customer or request category, assess ticket status based on comment threads, send public replies to customers, or add internal comments – all without leaving the chat.




Find company knowledge
Use Ask YouTrack to search your Knowledge Base and understand how teams and processes work across the company. For example, with a single prompt, colleagues can find the right person to contact, learn how things are organized, or get answers to common onboarding questions.




Use leading AI providers, your own API keys, or a custom model
On the AI Features page, administrators can choose OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google as their AI service provider, then select a specific model or use the recommended option. They can connect a JetBrains AI subscription, use their own provider API key (BYOK), or add a custom or locally hosted model compatible with one of the three providers. To help you get started, paid YouTrack Cloud subscriptions include a weekly allowance of AI credits.




Keep AI usage and credit spending under control
See how your team uses AI 
Administrators can monitor team members’ AI quota usage on the AI Features page. Usage for the current month is broken down by user and feature, including Ask YouTrack, AI Actions, link suggestions, and comment suggestions. Free quota usage is shown as a percentage, with a breakdown of how that quota is used across features. For paid connections, YouTrack also shows estimated costs based on usage. Paid connections show estimated costs, while free quota usage is shown as a percentage. Actual charges may vary depending on your provider’s pricing. 
Built-in writing assistance – including grammar and spelling correction, text completion, and text recognition in uploaded files – remains free, does not consume quota, and runs exclusively on JetBrains infrastructure, powered by JetBrains AI.




New AI credit pricing for YouTrack Cloud and Server
Starting with this release, the built-in AI Assistant, which helps you summarize context and write text faster, uses a new pricing model. A limited number of AI credits are now included and replenished weekly with paid YouTrack Cloud subscriptions. YouTrack Cloud and YouTrack Server customers on free plans or with active paid subscriptions can access paid credits through a connected JetBrains AI subscription or use BYOK.
Expanded integrations for AI-assisted work in Slack, Claude, and ChatGPT
Task creation from Slack threads
The YouTrack Slack app can now use AI to create tasks from threads. For example, product teams can mention @YouTrack in a channel to turn a conversation into a feature request and specify what the task should include. Beyond AI, the Slack app can send you direct-message notifications about task and ticket updates and show task and article previews when you share YouTrack links.




Simpler YouTrack MCP setup for Claude and ChatGPT
In addition to OAuth authorization for compatible MCP clients, you can now connect YouTrack Cloud to Claude and ChatGPT directly through their respective directories. These connections let you work with tasks, tickets, articles, and project context without configuring MCP manually. The ChatGPT connection is available for Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces. Users on Pro and Plus plans can connect through MCP by adding a custom plugin.




If you prefer the terminal, the open-source YouTrack CLI is now available through package managers. Use it to manage work from the terminal, automate CI pipelines, and make AI agent workflows more token-efficient.
Whiteboards: Richer visuals and easier collaboration
Add visual context with images, frames, and lines
You can now upload or paste screenshots, mockups, and other images directly into your boards. Frames let you group related cards, tasks, and articles by project stage or arrange them in a Kanban-style layout. You can also draw lines to connect work items, with more shapes coming soon.




Clone boards and manage access
You can now clone whiteboards and reuse existing layouts for recurring planning sessions, roadmaps, or retrospectives. Whiteboards now also support keyboard shortcuts for faster editing.
New permission controls let administrators manage access to whiteboard content and settings separately. Team members can add and organize content, while only users with configuration access can change the board’s settings and sharing permissions.




Find and import content more easily
Improved search and import make it easier to find and add tasks, articles, and linked tasks directly to your boards. When you need to view tasks as a list, you can add native issue lists alongside other available YouTrack widgets.




Gantt chart improvements for flexible planning
Plan around deadlines and milestones
We’ve improved the Gantt chart experience – from initial planning to managing ongoing work. You can now configure a chart using three planning modes. When a project has a fixed release, delivery, or customer deadline, plan backward using task end dates and estimates. For projects with more flexible timelines, schedule tasks using start dates and estimates. If you already know both dates, start with the Start date and end date planning mode.
As your team makes progress, add milestones to highlight approvals, releases, and other important events. Mark tasks as milestones manually or automatically based on a field value or tag. You can also display selected custom fields, tags, and assignees for each task directly on the Gantt chart.




Navigate daily work and long-term plans
During project reviews, you can now jump to the current date to compare ongoing work with upcoming deadlines. Pan across the schedule and zoom between a detailed weekly view all the way out to  monthly, quarterly, and yearly overviews.




Improved reporter experience in YouTrack Helpdesk
More customers who already use YouTrack to manage projects and maintain documentation are also adopting YouTrack Helpdesk for support requests. Based on highly requested features, we’re continuing to improve YouTrack Helpdesk and making it easier to migrate from Zendesk, Trengo, and other helpdesk platforms. This release focuses on enhancing the experience for your reporters, including external customers and internal service desk users.
Send attachments in email notifications
Email notifications can now include files attached to tickets, tasks, and comments. Reporters can open screenshots, receipts, equipment photos, and other supporting materials directly from their email inboxes without opening the ticket in YouTrack. If you restrict a file’s visibility, only users with access will receive it by email. Files larger than 10 MB are included as links.




Manage email notifications for reporters
Administrators can now choose which built-in notifications reporters receive in each helpdesk project, reducing unnecessary emails. They can disable notifications for ticket creation, new public comments, and automated ticket reminders. For example, reporters can get an email when an agent replies in a public comment, but not when an agent creates a ticket on their behalf.




Set up new email channels faster
Administrators can now reuse an existing mailbox server to add another email channel without configuring the connection again. This is useful when Helpdesk expands to more products, departments, or service teams. We have also improved the email channel setup interface.
New YouTrack apps and developer updates
Develop YouTrack apps with AI agents
We’ve released the YouTrack Apps Agent Skill and an updated CLI for a smoother development experience with AI agents. You can build YouTrack apps and workflow rules directly in your IDE instead of relying only on the built-in editor. An agent can draft an app in minutes and keep its code in Git, while the CLI uploads it directly to the target YouTrack instance and project. This helps app developers deliver customizations and integrations for their own teams or clients several times faster. 
See how it works in this hands-on example from the YouTrack Reddit community, or hear from msp AG, an Honored YouTrack App Creator, about their experience building apps with AI agents. Read the msp AG case study to learn how the team replaced Jira add-ons with custom YouTrack apps after migrating to YouTrack.
“Building apps for YouTrack requires detailed knowledge of the YouTrack API and architectural planning, plus general technical understanding, but not necessarily deep programming knowledge. As a vibe coder, I managed to do most of this myself with some support from developers, and many tasks can be handled with Cursor, Windsurf, Junie, or other coding agents.”

            
Julian Radünz
                                                                Team Lead, Professional Services, MSP AG
                                    
Discover new apps from YouTrack Certified Partners and independent developers
The number of YouTrack apps on JetBrains Marketplace has almost doubled in just over half a year. Some apps add entirely new capabilities to YouTrack, while others make everyday work easier with smaller enhancements. Most apps are free, with paid options available for teams that need more advanced functionality.
Plan team capacity and project timelines
Panorama by twenty20 adds professional resource and capacity planning to a dedicated page in YouTrack. View your team’s workload on a timeline, compare planned hours with available capacity, and reschedule tasks by dragging and dropping them. The app is free during Early Access.




Calendar by twenty20 gives you a personal calendar in YouTrack to organize your project activity by date. Choose which projects and sprints from Agile boards to include. You can even switch between day, week, month, and year views.




Sprint Capacity Planner by Nikita Koval lets managers plan sprints around each person’s availability, drag and drop tasks from the backlog to assign them to team members, and create a new sprint in one click.




One Roadmap by Alex Basis lets you plan project work on a timeline by week, month, or quarter. Project managers can map existing date fields to the timeline and schedule tasks that don’t have exact dates yet.




Manage checklists and personal productivity
Checklists for YouTrack by Appfero turns recurring steps into reusable checklists for tasks and articles. Start with built-in templates or create your own, mark key steps as required, and keep tasks unresolved until their checklists are complete. This paid app includes a free 30-day trial.




Checklist Pro for YouTrack by Checklist Pro Labs gives each issue type, such as Task or Bug, its own checklist with required steps. The corresponding template is then automatically applied to new issues of the same type.




Real Quick Notes by J&J Ideenschmiede lets you keep quick notes, reminders, and to-dos directly on your YouTrack dashboard. The widget automatically saves everything you type. 




Configurable Issue List by Testcase lets you organize and access issues directly from your dashboard with the Dynamic Issue Table widget. Use a saved search or type in your own query. You can also choose which columns to display and filter the results.




Enhance task content with custom field layouts, warnings, and more
Fieldwise by twenty20 helps you organize long lists of custom fields more conveniently by arranging them into groups, tabs, and columns. Project admins can drag and drop fields to customize the layout, while team members edit values in place.




Fields+ by Medeu IT keeps key task details in view by showing the fields that matter most, such as priority, state, and assignee, right below the task summary. The free version uses one shared field list across all selected projects.




Lock by Marcus Christensson protects resolved tasks and Knowledge Base content from further edits by making them read-only until someone reopens the task or unfreezes the article.




Callouts by Maksim Fedorov makes warnings, tips, and key notes stand out in tasks and articles by writing GitHub-style alerts or using an editor toolbar.




Diffyt by Marcus Christensson lets you compare any two versions of a task or article line by line to see exactly what changed.




Track time and report on workloads
Effort Level Monitor by msp AG lets you know when a task takes longer than expected. Set time thresholds for each project, track logged time by effort level, and notify stakeholders with templated comments.




Adeptask Time Tracker by Adeptask lets you track time across several tasks with one-click timers that pause automatically when you start tracking another work activity. The app is free for up to 10 users, with a free 30-day trial available.




Adv.Weekly Report by mag1.cc lets you review your work week by week. Split a YouTrack search into calendar weeks on your dashboard and export weekly data to Excel for your status reports.




Enhance YouTrack administration capabilities
Instance Insights by Ninjaneers GmbH gives administrators a score out of 100 showing how well their instance has held up over time. The report can be exported or displayed on a dashboard.




Who Can Do What by Ninjaneers GmbH lets administrators see who holds which permissions across every project, group, and role. A dedicated YouTrack page lets them review access, mark permissions that should be removed, and export the results for an audit.




Adv.KVStore by mag1.cc lets you store settings, cached results, and sync state globally or per project through an HTTP API. Save data between app and workflow runs. 




Other enhancements
This release also brings improvements to the Notification Center, user profile and administration pages, time-tracking controls, and app configuration and management.
 
Check out the release notes for the full technical details and a comprehensive list of this release’s bug fixes and improvements. For more details on configuring the latest features, see the documentation.

posts.title: Mellum2.1 Instruct Is Out, Bringing Faster Answers for Coding Agents
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The faster sibling of Mellum2.1 Thinking, built for sub-agents, tool loops, and chat.
In October, we released Mellum2.1 Thinking, an open 12B mixture-of-experts model with 2.5B active parameters, trained to work as a coding agent. Today, we are releasing its sibling, Mellum2.1 Instruct. It is built on the same architecture and trained identically, but it gives straight answers without including its chain of thought.
What sets Mellum2.1 apart from Mellum2 is its post-training phase: large-scale reinforcement learning on repository-level tasks in real environments, built on NVIDIA NeMo open-source training libraries – NeMo RL and NeMo Megatron-Bridge for efficient large-scale distributed training.
As promised, this October we released the multi-token prediction (MTP) head for Mellum2.1 Thinking, making token generation up to 1.8x faster. Mellum2.1 Instruct is released together with its MTP head.
Try Mellum
Why an Instruct model, and when to use it
Reasoning models, such as Mellum2.1 Thinking, are a good fit for tasks that require a step-by-step approach, like finding the root cause of a failing test. But much of a coding agent’s work is simpler, like a small fix, a command to run, or a question about the code. In these cases, reasoning adds time and computing resources without adding quality.
This is especially true when the model runs locally – every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting. After the Thinking release, we received many requests from the local-inference community for a more concise model for moderately hard tasks.
That is where Mellum2.1 Instruct fits in – either on its own or as the fast worker next to a stronger model. On agentic coding tasks, it generates about half as many tokens as the Thinking variant and performs almost as well on SWE-bench Verified. On hard algorithmic and math problems, such as those in LiveCodeBench and AIME, thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice.
Performance on benchmarks
We compared Mellum2.1 Instruct with its predecessor, Mellum2 Instruct, and two open models in the same class, Qwen3.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B, both with thinking turned off.
The biggest gain is on the agentic benchmark SWE-bench Verified, where the score doubled compared with the previous Instruct release. The new training also improved code generation, where Mellum2.1 Instruct now leads the group, and multi-step tool use, where it is level with Qwen3.5 9B.
Qwen3.5 9B scores higher on SWE-bench Verified, but Mellum2.1 activates only 2.5B parameters per token. As a result, it generates tokens about 1.4x faster than Qwen3.5 9B for a single request and about 1.8x faster under load, as shown in our October post.




How we trained it
Mellum2.1 Instruct went through the same two reinforcement learning stages as Thinking. First, it learned to solve standalone tasks in code, math, tool use, and instruction following. Then it learned to work as an agent in real repositories, using shell and file tools inside a sandbox and being rewarded only when the hidden tests passed.
We made two adjustments for Instruct. We tuned the length penalty for a model that answers without thinking, which keeps its answers concise and reduces the number of tokens without sacrificing quality. We also brought generation and training into closer agreement, which makes training more stable.
Both stages are built on NVIDIA NeMo open-source training libraries. NeMo RL, a post-training library, runs generation and training asynchronously, and NeMo Megatron-Bridge handles the weight updates across the large-scale distributed clusters of NVIDIA H200 and B300 GPUs. Together they let a single run collect about half a million agent trajectories from 10,000 concurrent sandboxes.
This release builds on open research, frameworks, and datasets. That is why Mellum2.1 is also open for others to build on.
Get started with Mellum2.1
Both variants of Mellum2.1 are available on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. Each one also comes in two additional versions:
GGUF files for running the model on your own machine (Instruct, Thinking).
A multi-token prediction (MTP) head that makes generation up to 1.8x faster (Instruct, Thinking).
If you’re building coding agents, sub-agents, or AI tools that run on your own infrastructure, we’d love for you to try Mellum2.1. Tell us what works and what doesn’t in the comments below or in discussions on Hugging Face. Your feedback will shape the next version.
Try Mellum

posts.title: What Does JetBrains Do? The Essential Guide to Our Business
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
JetBrains builds tools developers use to write, check, and ship software, including tools that work with AI agents. You don’t need to be a coder to work here, but the specialists we hire are experienced in their fields, curious about technology, and ready to embrace AI. This guide explains what JetBrains does in plain language for anyone who has never heard of us or our products.
Where JetBrains technology shows up
88 of the Fortune Global 100 companies use JetBrains tools.
15M+ developers use JetBrains tools.
300K+ companies build with JetBrains.




What does JetBrains do? Most of our work happens behind the scenes, but the impact of our technology can be seen in products and services people use every day:
Netflix: Netflix engineers connected the engine that helps IntelliJ IDEA (our first product) understand code to their AI coding agents, enabling those agents to understand and modify Netflix’s software. They ran tests involving real programming tasks and found that the agents had become 20 to 30 percent more efficient, completing tasks faster and with fewer tokens (the units AI models are billed in). (JetBrains Blog, October 2026)
Google: More than 70 Google apps are built with Kotlin, the programming language created by JetBrains. These include Maps, Home, Play, Drive, and Messages. (Android Developers)
McDonald’s: The McDonald’s app uses Kotlin Multiplatform, a technology that lets developers share code between an app’s Android and iOS versions. (JetBrains Blog, KotlinConf’25; McDonald’s Technical Blog)




So what does JetBrains actually do? And why might it be an interesting place to work if you’re a recruiter, marketer, designer, finance professional, lawyer, salesperson, or workplace specialist? Let’s break it down.
What does JetBrains do?





We build tools developers and their teams use to write, check, and ship software, from websites and mobile apps to video games and banking systems. Our best-known tools are IDEs (integrated development environments). An IDE is a software application that combines everything a programmer needs to write, test, build, and debug code into one workspace.
Software is now also built with AI agents: programs that carry out multi-step tasks, such as fixing a bug, while a developer directs them.
To support this approach to development, we built Air, now available in our IDEs. Air gives developers one place to run agents such as Anthropic Claude Agent, OpenAI Codex, and JetBrains Junie. Developers can review the changes made by agents before accepting them. Air adds shared context, helping agents understand the project, plus permissions and spending limits.
But our product line isn’t limited to AI. We also build tools to help teams plan and manage their work (YouTrack), maintain code quality (Qodana), and automate testing and delivery (TeamCity). 
What does JetBrains do? Our revenue comes from subscriptions to our 30+ products. Individual developers and companies, from startups to large enterprises, pay to use our tools. We are a privately held company with no outside investors.
Where the business is heading
The field of software development is changing quickly. For 26 years, our IDEs have been where developers write code themselves. Now, AI agents are taking on more of that work. This raises an important question for every company that builds software: How do you make sure the software you ship is still good?
Our Developer Ecosystem Survey, now in its tenth year, shows us just how fast things are changing. Between May and July 2026, we asked more than 15,000 professional developers worldwide how they work:
90% use AI coding agents at work at least once a week, and 68% use them every day.
On average, developers estimate that AI agents wrote about 47% of the code they produced for work over the past month.
Senior developers are among the first to hand coding over to agents, with about a quarter of them reporting that agents write more than 80% of their code.
These figures are self-reported, and the results have been statistically reweighted to represent the worldwide development community. You can further explore these findings in these two posts from the JetBrains Research blog: AI Coding Agents: Adoption Trends and How Much Code Do Developers Really Let Agents Write?
Agents can write code fast, but creating quality software is about more than writing code. Developers still need context to guide agents and ways to review agent output, and someone has to take responsibility for the final product. We built Air as a response to this shift in the market and in our users’ needs. Companies also need control over how AI is used: which models, who can do what, and what it costs. Air supports this through permissions, spending limits, analytics, and AI policies.
We are not tied to any particular cloud provider or AI model vendor. Our customers pick the models and agents that work best for them, and we make product decisions based on their needs.
There is still a lot to figure out. Adoption, pricing, and the economics of AI are still evolving – and we’re still learning and adapting. This work involves the whole company, not just the engineering teams.
Who works at JetBrains besides developers?
JetBrains was founded by developers, and engineering remains at the heart of the company. But building successful technical products takes much more than engineering. It also takes people who understand the market, communicate the value of our products, support our users, negotiate agreements, manage budgets, hire the right people, organize events, run offices, and build partnerships.
About 3,000 people from more than 75 countries work at 15 offices, with English as our shared working language.
AI is finding its way into all kinds of roles at JetBrains. Here are a few examples of the impact AI is making outside of engineering:
“The biggest thing since sliced bread? For legal teams, AI is making a pretty strong case. We’re experimenting with self-service tools and agents that answer everyday legal questions. That’s what I enjoy: having room to rethink how legal works alongside people who are excited to try things.” Kristyna Jaros Tran, Legal Operations Team Lead, JetBrains
“Critical thinking is key: questioning the output, verifying it, and recognizing when AI gets it wrong.” Magda Rauner, Talent Acquisition, JetBrains
“Claude and Gemini are tools that are used daily in the Compensation & Benefits team for project planning, data analysis, and modeling. But my favorite feature is the Slack bot that can be added to channels to find answers or refer you to the right people.” Anna Fedosova, HR Principal Project Manager, JetBrains
Careers at JetBrains: What you need to bring
You don’t need to know how to read code. You do need to be curious about the market and its trends, enjoy working in a technical space, and have a commitment to keep learning as you go.
We hire experienced professionals. Our teams are small, so your work and your input are visible from day one. We hire you for your expertise in your own field, expecting that you will be able to build your technical knowledge on the job, with help from tech-savvy colleagues who are eager to share what they know. This applies to roles in legal, finance, marketing, hiring, and every other function outside engineering.
AI is changing how every team works. You will be expected to keep up and to think about how your team can use AI effectively. Nobody has all the answers from day one, not even people in technical roles. What matters is being willing to ask questions and understand the bigger picture: what a product does, who pays for it, and why it matters.
Want to learn more about working at JetBrains? Explore our locations, find out how we hire.
What you gain from working in tech
The people at JetBrains care about how things come together, not just whether they work. And this attention to quality goes beyond engineering – it also includes clear writing, thoughtful hiring, careful financial planning, and well-organized events.
What does JetBrains do? The JetBrains Fit Test describes autonomy as an important part of working here. People are trusted to draw upon their expertise, question existing approaches, and find better ways to do things.






Working close to technology can even change how you approach your own profession. Recruiters gain a deeper understanding of how technical teams work. Communicators learn to find the human story behind complex products. Financial and legal professionals see where speed matters and where taking a more careful approach protects long-term progress.
You don’t become less of a specialist. You become a specialist with a better understanding of the environment where your work creates value.
Software shapes much of the modern world. But developers alone aren’t enough to make this happen. A whole community is needed to explain it, support it, challenge it, organize around it, and help it reach the people who need it.
You could be a part of that community.
Further reading: From the Big 4 to Global Tech: What Changes When You Move In-House?

Register for the livestream

See how the AI Agents plugin lets you run AI tasks as part of CI. We’ll look at practical scenarios such as reviewing code and working with failed or flaky tests.

4. Configure Pipelines visually or in YAML

5. Improve GitHub pull-request workflows
We’ll cover connecting GitHub, reporting useful status checks, canceling outdated builds when new commits arrive, and working with merge queues.
We’ll also look at other release highlights, including Maven 4 support, and answer your questions live.
Speaking to you
Nikita Koshcheev, TeamCity Cloud Team Lead
Nikita has 14 years of experience in infrastructure engineering and DevOps. Before joining JetBrains to build the TeamCity Cloud service, he helped develop platforms in industries including eCommerce and fintech.

posts.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: Update Your JetBrains IDEs, ReSharper, .NET Tools, Toolbox App, and Gateway Now
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Summary
A critical security issue named Java4Shell was identified in OpenJDK, the basis of JetBrains Runtime (JBR), which is bundled with all JetBrains IDEs, ReSharper, the JetBrains Toolbox App, and Gateway.
The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and presents the weakness CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).
If abused, the flaw may enable an attacker to crash the IDE or, in the worst case, execute code remotely on your machine. 
Only IDEs running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support are exposed. ARM64, including Apple Silicon, is not affected.
The IDE updates listed below mitigate the issue for every supported release line. We encourage all users to update to the latest versions.
If you cannot update yet, a one-line VM option removes the exposure.
You must update the Java runtimes that your projects use for builds, tests, and run configurations separately, as they are not covered by IDE updates.
Details
On November 17, 2026, Oracle and the OpenJDK project released fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM. The issue was reported by Calif and is known as Java4Shell. 
To decode Base64 faster, HotSpot uses an intrinsic routine on x86-64 CPUs that support AVX-512 VBMI. Malformed input makes this routine write past the end of a Java array and corrupt neighboring memory. The reporters demonstrated how this routine could be exploited to execute arbitrary code in several server-side Java applications. OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, along with the 21, 25, and 27 lines, are affected across Java distributions. Oracle’s Java SE 8 Performance Pack (8u511-perf and earlier) is also affected, while standard Java 8 and Java 11 builds are not.
Every JetBrains IDE bundles JetBrains Runtime, which is based on OpenJDK. All current releases that bundle JBR 17 (17.0.6 and later), 21, or 25 are affected. This includes IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, GoLand, Rider, CLion, RubyMine, RustRover, DataGrip, and the JetBrains HTTP Client CLI, as well as remote development backends.
An IDE is exposed only if both of the following conditions are true: It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Xeon processors from Ice Lake onward, some tenth- and eleventh-generation Intel Core processors, or AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer; and it decodes Base64 data controlled by an attacker, for example, data received from a network peer.
At the time of publication, we are not aware of this vulnerability having been exploited against JetBrains IDEs.
The updates listed below mitigate the issue by adding the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option to the default VM options of all JetBrains IDEs. The option turns off the vulnerable routine for every use of java.util.Base64 in the IDE process. Base64 decoding then falls back to the regular Java implementation, which may be slower. The option is accepted on every platform. The upstream fix is being integrated into JetBrains Runtime separately, and we will update this post when new runtime builds are available.
The mitigation is included in the following IDE versions:

IDE2026.32026.22026.12025.32025.2
CLion2026.3.0.22026.2.5.12026.1.5.32025.3.6.42025.2.6.4
DataGrip2026.3.0.12026.2.7.12026.1.4.22025.3.6.22025.2.6.2
DataSpell——2026.1.3.22025.3.3.22025.2.4.2
Gateway2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.4.12025.3.3.12025.2.6.1
GoLand2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.5.32025.2.6.4
IntelliJ IDEA2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.5
PhpStorm2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4
PyCharm2026.3.0.22026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4
Rider2026.3.0.22026.2.5.12026.1.5.42025.3.6.42025.2.6.3
RubyMine2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4
RustRover2026.3.1.12026.2.6.12026.1.4.22025.3.7.22025.2.6.2
WebStorm2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4





Toolbox App needs to be updated to 3.9.2.
ReSharper needs to be updated to one of the following versions: 2026.3.0.2, 2026.2.5.1, 2026.1.5.4, 2025.3.5.4, or 2025.2.6.3.
How to protect yourself
Update your IDE. Download the latest version of your IDE from the JetBrains website or use the automatic update option in the Toolbox App or in Help | Check for Updates.
If you cannot update yet, apply the workaround. Open Help | Edit Custom VM Options, add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics on a new line, save the file, and restart the IDE. Do not use -XX:UseAVX=2 with JetBrains IDEs, even though some public advisories suggest it, as doing so will prevent JBR 25 from starting on ARM64.
Update the Java runtimes used by your projects. The IDE update only covers the IDE process. Build and run processes that use a project JDK, such as Gradle and Maven daemons, tests, and run configurations, are not covered. Update those JDKs to your vendor’s fixed build, for example, Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1. Other vendors, including Eclipse Temurin and Amazon Corretto, use their own build numbers, so check the vendor advisory. Until you can update, you can start those JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a workaround.
Check your exposure and confirm the option is active. If you use Linux, you can see whether your CPU supports AVX-512 VMBI by following the instructions in the Affected products section of the Calif write-up. To confirm that a running IDE uses the option, run jcmd <pid> VM.flags. This is useful if you maintain a custom VM options file or run a remote development backend.
The IDE updates and the workaround address only the vulnerability described above. We always recommend using the latest IDE version to benefit from other security updates.
For the upstream advisories and the write-up from the reporters, see:
OpenJDK Vulnerability Advisory: 2026/11/17
Oracle Critical Security Patch Update Advisory – November 2026
Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere by Calif
A complete list of recently fixed security issues is available on the Fixed security issues page on the JetBrains website. You can also subscribe to receive notifications about fixes in all JetBrains products via email.
Frequently asked questions
Which versions are affected?
All JetBrains IDE versions that bundle JBR 17 (17.0.6 and later), 21, or 25 are affected until they are updated to the versions listed above, or until the workaround is applied. An IDE is exposed only on x86-64 hardware with AVX-512 VBMI. We recommend upgrading as soon as possible.
Is it possible to backport the fix to other versions?
We are not considering backports to older IDE versions. The workaround described above prevents this issue and is compatible with them.
I use remote development. What should I do?
The remote IDE backend is an IDE process and receives the same default VM options as desktop IDE builds with the update. Remote hosts are often cloud x86-64 machines that support AVX-512 VBMI, so be sure to update the backend, or add the option to its custom VM options in the meantime.
I already added the option manually. Do I need to remove it once I update to a new version?
No. After you update, the option is one of the default VM options, so the manual entry is redundant but harmless. We will remove the default option once the IDEs bundle a version of JetBrains Runtime that contains the upstream fix.
Support
If you have any questions regarding this issue or encounter problems updating, please get in touch with the JetBrains Support team by submitting a ticket.

posts.title: Kotlin Benchmark 2.0: How AI Coding Agents Handle Harder Tasks and Closed-Source Code
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
In July, we released the Kotlin Benchmark – a collection of 105 real repository-level tasks for evaluating AI coding agents’ work with Kotlin. Since then, we’ve updated it to be more representative of what Kotlin teams do, with more reliable results and more data to help you choose an agent-model configuration.
The new tasks require changes across multiple files, come from projects in different Kotlin domains, and include code from private repositories. To prevent reward hacking and improve the reliability of our results, we restricted network access when agents solve open-source tasks, so they can’t look up a fix that has already been published. We also set  30-minute-per-task resolution time limit for each configuration, balancing the additional time required to solve complex problems with the need for a manageable evaluation time.
See the latest Kotlin Benchmark results
What’s new 





Harder tasks: The collection of tasks now focuses on medium- and high-complexity problems that require multi-step reasoning, debugging, and changes across multiple files. Simple single-file edits have been filtered out.
Open-source and closed-source tasks: Of the 100 tasks, 70 come from open-source GitHub repositories and 30 from private JetBrains ones, where neither the code nor the fix is available online. The leaderboard shows the results for the full suite and for each group separately, allowing for a direct comparison of the configuration’s performance on public and private code.
Broader Kotlin domain coverage: The 70 open-source tasks now come from 25 repositories, and they span key Kotlin domains: 30 Android, 20 backend, 10 Kotlin Multiplatform, and 10 libraries and tools. The 30 closed-source tasks come from internal JetBrains server-side Kotlin projects.
Restricted network access to prevent reward hacking: Agents complete the open-source tasks without network access, so a configuration can’t inflate its score by looking up the published fix.
New models, including open ones: The evaluated lineup has changed and now includes open models – Kimi and DeepSeek, both running via OpenCode. If you’re considering an open model, you can compare it with closed ones on the same tasks. Every configuration runs the full suite three times, and the exact agent-model pairings, versions, and run settings are on the leaderboard.
Average cost, tokens, and steps per task: The leaderboard now displays the average cost, tokens, and number of steps per task, alongside resolution rate and latency, so you can see how resource-intensive each configuration is.
Stricter guardrails to prevent solution lookup
When benchmark tasks come from previously solved public issues, an agent can retrieve the existing fix instead of deriving one from the task and the codebase. This is known as reward hacking, and in our preliminary runs, we found agents were doing exactly that.
To prevent it, agents now solve the open-source tasks in a stricter sandbox with restricted network access. Only calls to the model itself are allowed as traffic. Dependencies are cached in advance, the repository history is hidden, and agents are explicitly informed that network access is disabled to prevent repeated attempts to access it. Network access remains available for solving closed-source tasks, because their fixes aren’t published anywhere.
These controls prevent agents from looking up solutions at runtime, but they don’t help rule out data contamination. The open-source repositories and their associated fixes may be part of a model’s training data. That’s the reason for the 30 closed-source tasks, which stay private. The methodology documents the evaluation setup and its limits.
The results
In the new evaluation, the best resolution rate on the full suite (combining both open- and closed-source tasks) comes from Claude Code with Opus 5.5, which posted a 75.3% resolution rate and an average cost of \$0.84 per task. The other 12 configurations resolved between 54.3% and 73.7% and cost between \$0.02 and \$3.14 per task.
For the open-source dataset, the highest-scoring configurations are Claude Code with Fable 5.1 (86.2%), followed by Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (84.8%) and Junie using Opus 5.5 and GPT 6 Luna (79.5%). However, the latter configurations offer a comparable score at lower average costs per task (\$0.68 and \$0.33, respectively, versus \$2.38).
On the closed dataset (consisting of Kotlin server-side tasks), Antigravity CLI with Gemini 3.8 Flash performed the best (60%, \$1.74 per task), closely followed by OpenCode with Deepseek V4.1 Flash (58.9%), which had a more moderate price tag of \$0.08 per task.
As you compare, keep in mind that the latest Kotlin Benchmark uses a different, harder task suite, so its scores are not comparable with the first release. A lower number here doesn’t mean a model got worse. Compare configurations within the same benchmark version.




Results shown here reflect the second public iteration of the Kotlin Benchmark. The leaderboard will be updated as newer model evaluations are added.
As before, a task counts as completed only when the generated patch passes the required tests, and the scores are a comparison signal, not a guarantee for every codebase. Use the leaderboard to shortlist configurations, and then validate them on representative tasks from your own projects.
What’s next
In the coming weeks, we plan to release follow-up materials for this benchmark iteration. Specifically, we will:
Analyze the agentic solutions for the open-source tasks and identify any that have potentially been contaminated (reproduced from memory).
Compile results that go beyond resolution rate: we will run Qodana, the static analysis tool from JetBrains, to determine whether agents introduced any bugs, security issues, or code smells with their solutions. 
The Kotlin Benchmark and the follow-up analyses are part of our own research on how agents work with Kotlin code. By studying how they complete these tasks and where they fail, we learn what to improve in Kotlin and its tooling.
If you’d like to help us improve Kotlin’s compatibility with AI tools, let us know where you run into trouble and use this form to share examples of where AI gives you a poor, incorrect, or unhelpful result when working with Kotlin.
To learn more, explore the leaderboard, read the methodology, or inspect the public tasks and harnesses on GitHub.
Further reading
The Kotlin Benchmark Leaderboard
The Kotlin Benchmark Methodology
Introducing the Kotlin Benchmark for AI Coding Agents
